1: # Workshop Calendar integration
2: 
3: ALE-430 and ALE-432 publish regular Workshops and Beginners' Workshops to the
4: committee calendar through one synchronization protocol. ALE-433 adds private
5: Calendar Invitations for newly confirmed regular Workshop places. ALE-434 and
6: ALE-435 use that same participant protocol for Stripe-paid and workshop-credit
7: Beginners' Workshop places. ALE-437 adds a read-only launch preview and explicit
8: activation for existing upcoming eligible attendees.
9: There is no Calendar administration screen.
10: 
11: ## Deployment boundary
12: 
13: The integration owns its event/control/recipient tables, with no changes to Workshop
14: payment tables and no source foreign keys. ALE-437 replaces the old pause flag
15: with target-bound activation fields. Apply migrations before running the new code.
16: Deleted sources deliberately leave their Calendar removal obligations behind.
17: 
18: **Sending is inactive by default.** Credentials and deployment alone do not
19: activate it. Set `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_ENVIRONMENT` to `isolated` or `production`,
20: then explicitly run the matching activation task after review. The durable
21: activation key binds that environment, both calendar IDs, and the OAuth client
22: ID; changing any of them returns sending to inactive until another explicit
23: activation.
24: 
25: The optional runtime credential names are:
26: 
27: - `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_CLIENT_ID`
28: - `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_CLIENT_SECRET`
29: - `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_REFRESH_TOKEN`
30: - `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_COMMITTEE_ID`
31: - `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_PARTICIPANT_ID`
32: 
33: `isolated` requires separate credentials and calendars with synthetic data. It
34: is not a production-data sanitizer. Production credentials, resources, and
35: Google acceptance checks are outside this implementation.
36: 
37: Run these only in an authorized operator session:
38: 
39: ```sh
40: cd apps/phoenix
41: mix dhc.workshop_calendar.preview
42: mix dhc.workshop_calendar.activate isolated
43: mix dhc.workshop_calendar.activate production
44: ```
45: 
46: Preview starts only its read dependencies and Repo, not the application or its
47: workers. It emits private JSON containing recipient PII and makes no Google,
48: database or job writes. Activation re-reads and locks the current sources; it
49: never accepts a saved preview as input. Required missing or invalid end/schedule data refuses the
50: entire activation atomically. Missing or invalid recipients remain per-place
51: follow-up and do not stop eligible recipients from being activated.
52: 
53: Provision them using the existing production secret-manager workflow, not checked
54: in configuration. Use a dedicated organizer owning **both** distinct calendars
55: and only `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.events.owned`. Calendar/ACL
56: administration and domain-wide delegation are not used. The integration does
57: not create calendars or manage sharing.
58: 
59: Share the committee calendar read-only with the Workspace committee group. Keep
60: the participant calendar restricted and unshared with that group. Review public
61: and inherited domain permissions separately: event guest-list flags are not a
62: calendar ACL. Google organizer/Workspace administrators retain privileged access.
63: 
64: ## Beginners' Workshop end-time readiness
65: 
66: Beginners' Workshops require explicit Dublin civil `startTime` and `endTime`
67: when scheduled or rescheduled. The additive column migration accepts unknown
68: (`null`) legacy end times. The follow-up data migration uses the club-approved
69: baseline of **start + six Dublin civil hours** for existing missing values,
70: including historical rows. This is a baseline, not a recovered historical
71: duration. Explicitly recorded end times are never overwritten. Starts at or
72: after 18:00 remain unknown because six hours would cross midnight; overnight
73: sessions are unsupported. Rolling back the data migration preserves values
74: and any later coordinator corrections.
75: 
76: After deployment and before a later Beginners' Workshop Calendar launch, run
77: `mix dhc.beginners_workshops.end_times` (read-only, no Google calls). Inspect
78: `Dhc.BeginnersWorkshops.end_time_report/1` in an authorized operator session,
79: then resolve each remaining upcoming row with the authorized
80: `{:backfill_end_time, workshop_id, %{end_time: "HH:MM"}}` command through
81: `Dhc.BeginnersWorkshops.execute/3`. Backfill changes no cutoff, offer-round,
82: email, or attendance policy. While sending is active, backfill records Calendar
83: intent just like scheduling and rescheduling; it never calls Google inline.
84: 
85: The separate Intake Email data migration adds an `endTime` chip to the six
86: schedule-bearing templates, retaining coordinator copy and existing chips.
87: If there is no start-time chip, it appends an end-time sentence instead. It
88: rechecks the shared 2,000-character worst-case measure before saving: a custom
89: body too close to the limit stops the deployment with its email type and
90: required size, rather than truncating copy or breaking email delivery. Shorten
91: that template in the existing editor and rerun the migration. Rollback keeps
92: the edited bodies; queued emails are not rewritten or resent. Remaining
93: unknown workshop ends render as `TBC`.
94: 
95: ## Ownership and recovery
96: 
97: Workshop operations commit identifier-only synchronization intent alongside the
98: source change. Google runs outside those transactions. The source-owned
99: `Dhc.Workshops.calendar_projection/1` and
100: `Dhc.BeginnersWorkshops.calendar_projection/1` exclude descriptions, participant
101: details, prices and notes. Source kind plus immutable ID distinguish the two
102: contexts even if their IDs match. Calendar content consists of title/status, time, venue and an
103: ordinary authenticated dashboard URL. Committee events have no guests and all
104: mutations use `sendUpdates=none`. Beginners' Workshops appear on scheduling,
105: independent of offers or payments, using the protected workshop Manage URL.
106: Their owner converts both Dublin civil times through Club Calendar. An unknown
107: or invalid legacy end never becomes a guessed duration or a malformed Google
108: event: it is reported without contacting Google. A source schedule correction
109: re-arms only this data failure, not a terminal Google/authorization failure.
110: 
111: The worker and five-minute repair pass share `Dhc.WorkshopCalendar.sync/3`.
112: Event identities and recreation generations are persisted before creation;
113: uncertain success is recovered by reading the same organizer event. Updates and
114: deletions use Google ETags. An event lease and source revision fence local
115: acknowledgments. Interrupted ownership expires after two minutes. Repair also
116: finds deleted-source work and missed wake-ups.
117: 
118: A persisted create checkpoint distinguishes an event never requested from an
119: insert that may still arrive after timeout. Never-requested deletions settle
120: locally. A 404 after a prepared create stays in repair until a tombstone or
121: successful delete proves that a late insert cannot leave a live event behind.
122: 
123: Temporary failures back off from 30 seconds and exhaust after six attempts.
124: Permanent or exhausted event failures retain their reason and episode and report
125: to Sentry. An episode is claimed under lock; best-effort capture follows commit,
126: never an uncommitted synchronization transaction. Sentry is monitoring, not a
127: guaranteed delivery ledger. Repair does not repeatedly call Google for terminal
128: failures; do not delete integration rows to retry, because that discards identity and cleanup
129: obligations. There is no pause/resume or manual recovery command. Domain commands
130: remain available with missing Google credentials or inactive sending.
131: 
132: Archival does not change Calendar. Cancellation retains the committee event at
133: its scheduled time, marked Cancelled; a cancelled source that was never published
134: does not acquire a new event at launch. Hard deletion removes the organizer event,
135: including after its end. First publication, detail repair and missing-event
136: recreation stop at the exact event end; owed cancellation/deletion still runs.
137: Early Beginners' Workshop attendance finalisation does not cancel, remove or
138: shorten its committee event; its scheduled end remains the publication cutoff.
139: 
140: ## Participant invitations
141: 
142: Regular Workshop payment completion captures the saved Registration address in
143: the same transaction that confirms the new place. Member addresses come from the
144: member snapshot, not PaymentIntent receipt/payer details. External addresses are
145: the participant details saved on the Registration; the legacy Checkout
146: `customer_email` fallback still supports booking identity but never fills a
147: missing participant snapshot or Calendar address. Pending Registrations,
148: unfinished Checkout and compensating payments do not qualify. Replayed payment
149: completion never captures another entitlement or selects a newer profile address.
150: 
151: Beginners' Workshop Stripe completion and workshop-credit confirmation capture
152: the locked Waitlist entry's recorded address only when the Intake actually
153: becomes paid. The person's Intake-link confirmation and the coordinator's
154: confirmation use the same command; it records the binding after applying the
155: credit in that transaction. Held credit and contacted places alone do not qualify,
156: and refused or repeated confirmations record no new entitlement. The retained
157: binding belongs to the integration, keyed by the Intake's immutable ID; neither
158: the Intake nor a delayed worker keeps/chooses another email snapshot. The
159: Checkout payer, frozen hold email and Guardian are not recipient sources.
160: Payment replays and repeated credit confirmations leave that binding unchanged.
161: Offers, open holds, failed or unpaid Checkout, policy failures and payments
162: refunded after the place closed do not create invitation entitlements. Google
163: failures cannot undo confirmation.
164: 
165: Beginners' Workshop Settlement rows record `:remove_calendar_place` for deferral,
166: withdrawal, cancel-with-refund and workshop cancellation alongside their existing
167: effects. Refund submission/completion is independent. Attendance finalisation and
168: corrections deliberately have no removal step, even when a no-show is corrected
169: to deferred: that is attendance history, not a prospective place withdrawal.
170: `calendar_place_ids/1` therefore reports confirmation facts (`paid_at`), including
171: historical Intakes; a retained binding's explicit removal obligation determines
172: place loss. This read never selects recipients or creates new entitlements.
173: Reschedule uses the same participant event, preserving surviving Google RSVPs.
174: Recipient failures retain one durable episode per failed place and report to
175: Sentry; they do not create capability/dashboard Notifications.
176: 
177: The integration retains each logical place and its selected address separately
178: from source storage, including failed addresses and owed removals. The shared
179: `sync/3` operation takes `audience: :participant`; identifier-only jobs include
180: that audience. Event identity/generation, leases, retries and failure episodes
181: are the same protocol as committee synchronization. Participant events have an
182: independent identity on the restricted calendar and contain only title, explicit
183: start/end and venue, plus Google event/guest metadata. Guests cannot see other
184: guests, edit the event or invite others. No dashboard links or descriptions are
185: exported.
186: 
187: Cancellation and refund requests record removal when the place ends, not when
188: Stripe completes its refund. Whole-workshop cancellation deletes the participant
189: event while retaining the Cancelled committee entry. Reconciliation reads Google
190: before replacing the attendee array and preserves surviving guest records/RSVPs.
191: Removals run before isolated additions; malformed or Google-rejected addresses
192: remain per-place follow-up and cannot block valid invitations. Terminal recipient
193: failures report to Sentry once per durable failure episode. No-op reconciliation is
194: silent; privacy-only repair does not notify guests. New invitations, meaningful
195: detail changes, guest removals and event cancellation use `sendUpdates=all`.
196: 
197: Attendance and archival preserve Calendar history. At/after the scheduled end,
198: there are no first invitations, detail rewrites or missing-event recreations.
199: Owed attendee removals and event cancellation still run. A Google-only RSVP
200: decline or removal of a personal copy is not a lost dashboard place or another
201: invitation entitlement. A new confirmed Registration or Intake after a lost place
202: is a new entitlement, including when loss and reconfirmation happened while sending was inactive.
203: Spending or forfeiting an applied workshop credit during attendance finalisation
204: does not remove historical invitations.
205: 
206: ## Person deletion and historical privacy cleanup (ALE-436)
207: 
208: The existing Beginners' Workshop manual Delete and three-month retention purge
209: capture privacy-removal obligations for every retained Intake binding before
210: anonymising or unlinking the person. They use the same authoritative transaction
211: and locks as before. Authorization, deletion refusals, refunds, anonymisation and
212: reporting are unchanged; Google never runs in that transaction and cannot delay
213: the person's deletion. There is no new Member/Principal deletion policy: those
214: records currently have no supported person hard-delete entrypoint. The shared
215: Calendar boundary accepts source-owned place identifiers for either source kind
216: when a supported operation needs it; it never finds people by matching email.
217: 
218: Obligations live on the integration's retained recipient rows, without source
219: foreign keys. Identifier-only jobs and periodic repair find them even after the
220: Waitlist entry/profile is gone. Inactive sending retains them without Google
221: mutations; activation reconciles current facts, not queued attendee snapshots.
222: Cleanup runs at and after event end, and even with an unknown legacy end time.
223: It removes the retained selected address from current and
224: historical organizer events, preserving other guests, their RSVPs and event
225: details. An address shared by another active entitlement remains that guest's
226: address; deleting one binding must not cancel the other's invitation.
227: 
228: Cleanup uses the event lease/revision and Google's conditional-write ETag. Even
229: when the guest is already absent, a conditional write advances the provider fence
230: before personal data is discarded, preventing an expired worker's late update
231: from restoring it. Ambiguous success is read back through the same bounded retry
232: and Sentry-reporting protocol. A tombstone or an event never requested can
233: settle without creation. A bare 404 after a prepared creation retains the
234: obligation: the uncertain insertion might still arrive. Cleanup never recreates
235: an event solely to remove someone, including after its end.
236: 
237: Once acknowledged under current ownership, cleanup clears the binding's selected
238: address, previous addresses and recipient failure data. It keeps only an inactive,
239: address-free place tombstone so stale confirmation retries cannot select an
240: address again. Event acknowledgments contain no attendee snapshots; jobs contain
241: no addresses or request bodies. A failed historical removal remains outstanding
242: for bounded reconciliation and Sentry reporting.
243: 
244: This cleans integration-owned organizer details only. It cannot guarantee erasure
245: of recipient calendar copies, delivered invitation emails or Google's retained
246: data. Neither successful HTTP responses nor cleanup acknowledgments promise
247: invitation email delivery or universal deletion.
248: 
249: ## Verification
250: 
251: Automated tests substitute Google and OAuth HTTP only through Req.Test; they
252: must never reach live Google. The ordinary Phoenix Testcontainers harness is
253: required for source/job/recovery/concurrency tests:
254:

256: cd apps/phoenix
257: mise exec -- mix test test/dhc/workshop_calendar test/dhc/workshops/calendar_projection_test.exs
258: mise exec -- mix precommit
259: ```

7: [Google Places terms validation](google-places-terms-validation.md). Its provider
8: requirements must be resolved within the confirmed venue-name search scope;
9: address-only autofill was rejected as a replacement. Manual destinations remain
10: available independently. The native Calendar goal below is unchanged.
11: 
12: ## Goal
13: 
14: Help attendees navigate to the right venue from their Calendar Invitation and
15: attendee-facing workshop page. Google autocomplete is an aid to selecting that
16: destination, not a requirement for scheduling a workshop.
17: 
18: Calendar integration is already implemented. This feature extends it rather
19: than introducing another Calendar delivery path. See
20: [the integration guide](workshop-calendar.md).
21: 
22: ## Agreed decisions
23: 
24: Confirmed on 6 November 2026:
25: 
26: - Keep ordinary Google Maps venue-name search: search for a venue, deliberately
27:   select a result, save the destination, and use it for directions and Calendar's
28:   native location. The user explicitly rejected an address-only downgrade and
29:   further product-scope questions about that choice. Resolve provider details
30:   within this scope rather than presenting speculative restrictions as a reason
31:   to redesign it.
32: - Cover regular Workshop create/edit and Beginners' Workshop schedule/reschedule.
33: - Keep the existing short venue label separate from the selected Google location.
34:   Beginners' Workshop labels retain their existing 80-character email limit.
35: - Let staff enter a venue/address manually if Google has no suitable result or is
36:   unavailable, with an optional manually supplied Maps link.
37: - Favour Dublin in suggestions without excluding other locations.
38: - Show directions in Calendar events and attendee-facing workshop pages.
39: - Use Calendar's native location field, not a Maps link added to the event
40:   description. The goal is a recognizable, navigable venue in the Calendar UI.
41: - Include backfill for existing upcoming workshops, including those outside the
42:   normal regular Workshop edit window. Use a one-off reviewed mapping from
43:   existing venue text to selected destinations, with a preview of every affected
44:   upcoming workshop. Never silently choose the first Google search result; leave
45:   ambiguous venues unchanged for review. Past workshops stay untouched.
46: - Backfill follows the normal Calendar attendee-update mechanism, accepting that
47:   Google may send update emails. Enriching the same venue's destination details
48:   does not trigger separate workshop-rescheduled emails or change its date/time.
49:   It does not authorize moving a published workshop to another physical venue.
50:   No production backfill has been authorized or run.
51: - Leave existing email templates unchanged. This does not suppress Calendar's
52:   existing attendee-update notifications.
53: - Do not add an embedded map, coordinates requirement or shared venue directory.
54: - Preserve the separation between Workshop and Beginners' Workshop storage and
55:   commands. Reuse the existing Calendar synchronization protocol.
56: 
57: ## Verified integration constraints
58: 
59: - `Dhc.WorkshopCalendar.Sync` currently puts the source projection's `location`
60:   into Google's event `location` field. Committee event descriptions contain the
61:   protected dashboard link; participant events export no description.
62: - Google's Calendar event `location` is free-form text, not a structured Place ID
63:   field. A name/address can populate it, but this alone does not guarantee that
64:   Calendar resolves the intended Google Place. The published Calendar discovery
65:   schema also exposes no ordinary-event structured Place field. Verify the native
66:   location/navigation experience on an authorized isolated calendar rather than
67:   promising exact Place identity based on an API write alone.
68: - Existing published-Workshop editing restrictions and Beginners' Workshop
69:   reschedule/email policies remain in force unless explicitly changed here.
70: - Google Places has attribution and storage restrictions, including EEA-specific
71:   terms. The persistence strategy must be checked against the applicable terms;
72:   do not assume all returned place details can be stored indefinitely.
73: - Places requires its own API/billing/key configuration; existing Calendar OAuth
74:   does not establish that Places is configured.
75: - The owner confirmed that the intended Google Maps billing account is based in
76:   Ireland/EEA. Use that account region for validation; the actual project and any
77:   account-specific agreement have not been inspected.
78: 
79: ## Authorization boundary
80: 
81: No interview policy questions remain open. The user confirmed the complete scope
82: summary. Design confirmation is not permission to implement the feature, provision
83: Google, activate production sending, or backfill production records.
84: 
85: ## Implementation and verification scope
86: 
87: - Reuse one autocomplete input across the ordinary Workshop form and the
88:   Beginners' Workshop schedule/reschedule forms, preserving remote-form bindings,
89:   keyboard access, field errors and manual fallback.
90: - Extend each domain's own storage, request/read contracts and Calendar projection
91:   without merging their commands or tables. Regenerate the typed API client.
92: - Add attendee-facing directions links without exporting private Intake links,
93:   tokens or roster details to Google.
94: - Use the existing Calendar protocol for destination updates, preserving event
95:   identities, attendees, RSVPs, retry/fencing behaviour and historical cutoffs.
96: - Provide a preview/apply backfill through authorized source-owned operations,
97:   re-checking current rows before applying reviewed mappings. Do not bypass
98:   domain command ownership with direct database updates.
99: - Test form submissions, manual/failure paths, both API contracts, projections,
100:   backfill preview/application, normal Calendar update notifications and the
101:   absence of separate workshop-rescheduled emails for venue enrichment.
102: - Run affected frontend build/typecheck/lint/unit/browser/E2E coverage, Phoenix
103:   precommit and API generation/idempotency checks during implementation. Automated
104:   tests substitute Google; isolated live-Calendar acceptance requires separate
105:   authorization and synthetic data.
106: 
107: Provisional effort: 3–5 developer days, excluding Google provisioning and human
108: venue review. Native Calendar navigation behaviour and the applicable Places
109: storage terms remain technical validation gates, not claims already verified by
110: the design interview.
111: 
112: ## Sources
113: 
114: - [Google Calendar Events resource](https://developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/v3/reference/events#location)
115: - [Google Places policies](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/policies)
116: - [Calendar specification, ALE-429](https://linear.app/alessandrojcm/issue/ALE-429/spec-workshop-calendar-and-calendar-invitations)
117: - [Current Calendar launch scope, ALE-437](https://linear.app/alessandrojcm/issue/ALE-437/calendar-launch-preview-and-explicit-activation)

This is a web application written using the Phoenix web framework.

## Project guidelines

- Use `mix precommit` when you are done and fix pending issues. Its alias must keep `hex.audit` first because dependency-provided tasks unload archived Hex tasks from the current Mix process; it then runs Credo, `reach.check --arch`, compilation, formatting, and tests.
- Production Docker tool versions still come from root `.mise.toml`, projected by `tools/phoenix-toolchain-config.sh`. Keep projection in its separate `toolchain-config` stage and copy only `beam.toml`/`runtime.toml` into install stages; projecting inside an install stage would still rebuild OTP after unrelated mise edits.
- Legacy end times have one approved deployment exception: the ALE-431 data migration fills missing values (historical rows included) with start + six civil hours, preserving explicit ends and leaving starts at/after 18:00 unknown. Operational backfills still use `execute/3`'s authorized `backfill_end_time` command before the Dublin start instant; known-time corrections use reschedule. Neither backfill changes deadlines or attendance policy; see `docs/workshop-calendar.md`.
- Workshop Calendar source changes call `Dhc.WorkshopCalendar.record_change/2` or `record_deleted/2` inside their existing transaction; integration rows retain identity and cleanup after source deletion, and an absent Google event is not proof that a timed-out insert cannot arrive later. Read `docs/workshop-calendar.md` before changing reconciliation or enabling sends.
- Regular Workshop Calendar Invitations capture the saved participant address with `confirm_place/4` in the new-confirmation branch of PaymentCommands or the source-locked launch backfill; its legacy Checkout payer fallback is not a participant address. One Google guest can serve several logical places, so removing one binding preserves another active binding's guest and RSVP; see the participant protocol in `docs/workshop-calendar.md`.
- Beginners' Workshop Calendar projections keep early-finalised workshops scheduled: only the explicit scheduled end stops publication and repair, not attendance finalisation. Unknown legacy ends remain `nil`; schedule/backfill commands re-arm that data failure through the shared Calendar intent, never by guessing a duration.
- Beginners' Workshop Calendar Invitations bind the locked Waitlist email when an Intake becomes paid (Stripe completion or credit confirmation in `IntakeCommands`, shared by person and staff) or through the source-locked launch backfill; held credit and confirmation replays create no entitlement. Explicit lost-place Settlement rows own `:remove_calendar_place`. `calendar_place_ids/1` reads confirmation history, not current attendance state: keep attendance corrections (including no-show → deferred) removal-free. See `docs/workshop-calendar.md` for the shared participant protocol.
- Person deletion records `WorkshopCalendar.forget_places/2` before Intake anonymisation, inside `Commands.People`'s existing locked transaction. Keep its address-free binding tombstones: cleanup scrubs addresses only after fenced Google acknowledgment, including after event end; place cancellation alone does not erase them. See `docs/workshop-calendar.md` for privacy recovery and external-copy limits.
- Calendar launch (ALE-437) is `mix dhc.workshop_calendar.preview` then explicit `activate isolated|production`, matching `WORKSHOP_CALENDAR_ENVIRONMENT`; only target-bound database activation enables non-test sending. Preview loads `app.config` and a temporary Repo, never `app.start`, which would wake workers. Keep source materialization inside PaymentCommands/Commands.CalendarLaunch and existing bindings immutable. The narrowed scope keeps automatic sync/retries but claims terminal failure episodes durably before best-effort post-commit Sentry capture, not dashboard Notifications; pause/resume and manual recipient-correction APIs are removed. See `docs/workshop-calendar.md`.
- Training Calendar sharing belongs to `Dhc.TrainingCalendar`, with its own ACL-only OAuth credential and grant ledger; keep it separate from Workshop Calendar's event-only authorization. Read `docs/training-calendar.md` before changing sharing ownership, the Dublin-midnight Cron gate, or enablement.
- Waitlist entry positions are numbered across the full selected standing before search or cursor filtering; `totalCount` still counts only search matches. Keep search outside `positioned_entries_query/1`'s subquery in `Dhc.Waitlist`.
- Waitlist `last_contacted` means the latest queued email, not confirmed delivery. `IntakeEmails.deliver/5` advances it monotonically through `Dhc.Waitlist.record_contact/2` after queueing and logging; every emailing command must lock the recipient's Waitlist entry before Intake/payment rows, including reschedule and follow-up passes.
- Keep Bandit at `~> 1.14` or newer within the compatible minor line; 1.12.5 fixes CVE-2026-74836/75484 and 1.14.0 fixes the October-2026 HTTP/2 and WebSocket set (CVE-2026-108525, -109584, -110314, -110499, -111101, -111103, -113436, -114213, -114216, -115269). plug_crypto must stay at `~> 2.2.1` (CVE-2026-105963: guard failures leaked the secret key base into logs).
- Run `mix credo --all` from `apps/phoenix` for static analysis; the project configuration also enables `ExSlop`
- Reach enforces module boundaries in `.reach.exs`: web→Repo only via `DhcWeb.Plugs.MagicLinkRateLimit`, Stripe only via `Dhc.Stripe.Operations.*` (never `Dhc.Stripe.Client.request/1`), Nostrum only inside `Dhc.Discord.*`, Req as the only HTTP client, no `IO.puts` outside Mix tasks/`Dhc.Release`. New findings fail the build; baseline known transitional findings with `MIX_ENV=dev mix reach.check --arch --write-baseline .reach-baseline.json`
- **Stripe test seam (ALE-342)**: every Stripe HTTP call goes through `Dhc.Stripe.Client` (via `Dhc.Stripe.Operations.*`), which merges `:stripe_req_options`; tests run it against `plug: {Req.Test, Dhc.Stripe}`. Stub Stripe HTTP with `Dhc.StripeHTTPStub` (`stub/3`, `expect/4`, `form/1`, `json/3`) — no Bypass, and tests never `put_env` `:stripe_api_url`, `:stripe_secret_key` or `:stripe_req_options`. Workshop tests pick one of three seams: `Dhc.StripeHTTPStub` for a test that stubs a few Stripe routes; `DhcWeb.WorkshopStripeClient` (a whole-Stripe `Req.Test` plug, `Req.Test.stub(Dhc.Stripe, DhcWeb.WorkshopStripeClient)`) for workshop controller contract tests that should run the live adapter; and `Dhc.Workshops.StripeStub` (the `:workshop_stripe_adapter`, app-env driven) for `PaymentCommands` workflow tests whose Stripe call runs outside the test's `$callers` tree (unboxed concurrency tasks) or must be paused. The one exception: real-Stripe `:integration` suites `put_env` a real `:stripe_secret_key` and reset `:stripe_req_options` to `[]` in setup (and restore both on exit); no other test changes Stripe config. Stubs reach Tasks/inline jobs via `$callers`; other processes need `Req.Test.allow/3`. Shared subscription-payment decoding lives in `Dhc.Stripe.SubscriptionPayment` and the one retry rule in `Dhc.Stripe.Failure.retryable?/1`; see "Stubbing Stripe" in `docs/agents/notes.md`.
- Keep generated Stripe modules under `lib/dhc/stripe/generated/` excluded from Credo instead of refactoring generated source
- Use the already included and available `:req` (`Req`) library for HTTP requests, **avoid** `:httpoison`, `:tesla`, and `:httpc`. Req is included by default and is the preferred HTTP client for Phoenix apps
- **Documented exception (ADR 0021)**: transactional email goes through Swoosh, whose api client is `config :swoosh, api_client: Dhc.Email.ApiClient` wrapping `Swoosh.ApiClient.Finch` over a named `{Finch, name: Swoosh.Finch}` child in `Dhc.Application`. Finch is already a production dependency, so Hackney stays out of prod. Application code outside `Dhc.Email.*` still uses Req everywhere else.
- Hackney is test-only because Testcontainers requires its 1.x Unix-socket transport. Keep it out of production and do not force Hackney 4 until Testcontainers supports Docker Unix sockets with it; the matching Hackney advisory exceptions in `mix.exs` apply only to that test dependency.
- Nostrum's REST client pulls Gun and Cowlib into production (Gun is floored at 2.7 in `mix.exs`, which resolves Cowlib 2.21 — fixed for CVE-2026-43971 and CVE-2026-43969). Limit Cowlib advisory exceptions to explicitly reviewed CVE IDs and document the relevant exposure or mitigation in `mix.exs`; keep ignoring CVE-2026-43966 only until a fixed Cowlib release ships, and keep the Hackney 4-only CVE exceptions (CVE-2026-47069/47071/47075/47076) only while Testcontainers requires Hackney 1.x.

### Phoenix v1.8 guidelines

- **Always** begin your LiveView templates with `<Layouts.app flash={@flash} ...>` which wraps all inner content
- The `MyAppWeb.Layouts` module is aliased in the `my_app_web.ex` file, so you can use it without needing to alias it again
- Anytime you run into errors with no `current_scope` assign:
  - You failed to follow the Authenticated Routes guidelines, or you failed to pass `current_scope` to `<Layouts.app>`
  - **Always** fix the `current_scope` error by moving your routes to the proper `live_session` and ensure you pass `current_scope` as needed
- Phoenix v1.8 moved the `<.flash_group>` component to the `Layouts` module. You are **forbidden** from calling `<.flash_group>` outside of the `layouts.ex` module
- Out of the box, `core_components.ex` imports an `<.icon name="hero-x-mark" class="w-5 h-5"/>` component for hero icons. **Always** use the `<.icon>` component for icons, **never** use `Heroicons` modules or similar
- **Always** use the imported `<.input>` component for form inputs from `core_components.ex` when available. `<.input>` is imported and using it will save steps and prevent errors
- If you override the default input classes (`<.input class="myclass px-2 py-1 rounded-lg">)`) class with your own values, no default classes are inherited, so your
custom classes must fully style the input


<!-- usage-rules-start -->

<!-- phoenix:elixir-start -->
## Elixir guidelines

- Elixir lists **do not support index based access via the access syntax**

  **Never do this (invalid)**:

      i = 0
      mylist = ["blue", "green"]
      mylist[i]

  Instead, **always** use `Enum.at`, pattern matching, or `List` for index based list access, ie:

      i = 0
      mylist = ["blue", "green"]
      Enum.at(mylist, i)

- Elixir variables are immutable, but can be rebound, so for block expressions like `if`, `case`, `cond`, etc
  you *must* bind the result of the expression to a variable if you want to use it and you CANNOT rebind the result inside the expression, ie:

      # INVALID: we are rebinding inside the `if` and the result never gets assigned
      if connected?(socket) do
        socket = assign(socket, :val, val)
      end

      # VALID: we rebind the result of the `if` to a new variable
      socket =
        if connected?(socket) do
          assign(socket, :val, val)
        end

- **Never** nest multiple modules in the same file as it can cause cyclic dependencies and compilation errors
- **Never** use map access syntax (`changeset[:field]`) on structs as they do not implement the Access behaviour by default. For regular structs, you **must** access the fields directly, such as `my_struct.field` or use higher level APIs that are available on the struct if they exist, `Ecto.Changeset.get_field/2` for changesets
- Elixir's standard library has everything necessary for date and time manipulation. Familiarize yourself with the common `Time`, `Date`, `DateTime`, and `Calendar` interfaces by accessing their documentation as necessary. The one sanctioned date/time dependency is `tz`, the IANA database behind `Dhc.ClubCalendar`'s Europe/Dublin conversions. **Never** install additional dependencies unless asked or for date/time parsing (which you can use the `date_time_parser` package)
- Don't use `String.to_atom/1` on user input (memory leak risk)
- Predicate function names should not start with `is_` and should end in a question mark. Names like `is_thing` should be reserved for guards
- Elixir's builtin OTP primitives like `DynamicSupervisor` and `Registry`, require names in the child spec, such as `{DynamicSupervisor, name: MyApp.MyDynamicSup}`, then you can use `DynamicSupervisor.start_child(MyApp.MyDynamicSup, child_spec)`
- Use `Task.async_stream(collection, callback, options)` for concurrent enumeration with back-pressure. The majority of times you will want to pass `timeout: :infinity` as option

## Mix guidelines

- Read the docs and options before using tasks (by using `mix help task_name`)
- To debug test failures, run tests in a specific file with `mix test test/my_test.exs` or run all previously failed tests with `mix test --failed`
- `mix deps.clean --all` is **almost never needed**. **Avoid** using it unless you have good reason

## Test guidelines

- **Always use `start_supervised!/1`** to start processes in tests as it guarantees cleanup between tests
- **Avoid** `Process.sleep/1` and `Process.alive?/1` in tests
  - Instead of sleeping to wait for a process to finish, **always** use `Process.monitor/1` and assert on the DOWN message:

      ref = Process.monitor(pid)
      assert_receive {:DOWN, ^ref, :process, ^pid, :normal}

   - Instead of sleeping to synchronize before the next call, **always** use `_ = :sys.get_state/1` to ensure the process has handled prior messages
<!-- phoenix:elixir-end -->

<!-- phoenix:phoenix-start -->
## Phoenix guidelines

- Remember Phoenix router `scope` blocks include an optional alias which is prefixed for all routes within the scope. **Always** be mindful of this when creating routes within a scope to avoid duplicate module prefixes.

- You **never** need to create your own `alias` for route definitions! The `scope` provides the alias, ie:

      scope "/admin", AppWeb.Admin do
        pipe_through :browser

        live "/users", UserLive, :index
      end

  the UserLive route would point to the `AppWeb.Admin.UserLive` module

- `Phoenix.View` no longer is needed or included with Phoenix, don't use it
<!-- phoenix:phoenix-end -->

<!-- phoenix:ecto-start -->
## Ecto Guidelines

- **Always** preload Ecto associations in queries when they'll be accessed in templates, ie a message that needs to reference the `message.user.email`
- Remember `import Ecto.Query` and other supporting modules when you write `seeds.exs`
- `Ecto.Schema` fields always use the `:string` type, even for `:text`, columns, ie: `field :name, :string`
- `Ecto.Changeset.validate_number/2` **DOES NOT SUPPORT the `:allow_nil` option**. By default, Ecto validations only run if a change for the given field exists and the change value is not nil, so such as option is never needed
- You **must** use `Ecto.Changeset.get_field(changeset, :field)` to access changeset fields
- Fields which are set programmatically, such as `user_id`, must not be listed in `cast` calls or similar for security purposes. Instead they must be explicitly set when creating the struct
- **Always** invoke `mix ecto.gen.migration migration_name_using_underscores` when generating migration files, so the correct timestamp and conventions are applied
<!-- phoenix:ecto-end -->

<!-- usage-rules-end -->

Keep source materialization inside PaymentCommands/Commands.CalendarLaunch and existing bindings immutable. The narrowed scope keeps automatic sync/retries but claims terminal failure episodes durably before best-effort post-commit Sentry capture, not dashboard Notifications; pause/resume and manual recipient-correction APIs are removed. See `docs/workshop-calendar.md`.
- Training Calendar sharing belongs to `Dhc.TrainingCalendar`, with its own ACL-only OAuth credential and grant ledger; keep it separate from Workshop Calendar's event-only authorization. Read `docs/training-calendar.md` before changing sharing ownership, the Dublin-midnight Cron gate, or enablement.
- Waitlist entry positions are numbered across the full selected standing before search or cursor filtering; `totalCount` still counts only search matches. Keep search outside `positioned_entries_query/1`'s subquery in `Dhc.Waitlist`.
- Waitlist `last_contacted` means the latest queued email, not confirmed delivery. `IntakeEmails.deliver/5` advances it monotonically through `Dhc.Waitlist.record_contact/2` after queueing and logging; every emailing command must lock the recipient's Waitlist entry before Intake/payment rows, including reschedule and follow-up passes.
- Keep Bandit at `~> 1.14` or newer within the compatible minor line; 1.12.5 fixes CVE-2026-74836/75484 and 1.14.0 fixes the October-2026 HTTP/2 and WebSocket set (CVE-2026-108525, -109584, -110314, -110499, -111101, -111103, -113436, -114213, -114216, -115269). plug_crypto must stay at `~> 2.2.1` (CVE-2026-105963: guard failures leaked the secret key base into logs).
- Run `mix credo --all` from `apps/phoenix` for static analysis; the project configuration also enables `ExSlop`
- Reach enforces module boundaries in `.reach.exs`: web→Repo only via `DhcWeb.Plugs.MagicLinkRateLimit`, Stripe only via `Dhc.Stripe.Operations.*` (never `Dhc.Stripe.Client.request/1`), Nostrum only inside `Dhc.Discord.*`, Req as the only HTTP client, no `IO.puts` outside Mix tasks/`Dhc.Release`. New findings fail the build; baseline known transitional findings with `MIX_ENV=dev mix reach.check --arch --write-baseline .reach-baseline.json`
- **Stripe test seam (ALE-342)**: every Stripe HTTP call goes through `Dhc.Stripe.Client` (via `Dhc.Stripe.Operations.*`), which merges `:stripe_req_options`; tests run it against `plug: {Req.Test, Dhc.Stripe}`. Stub Stripe HTTP with `Dhc.StripeHTTPStub` (`stub/3`, `expect/4`, `form/1`, `json/3`) — no Bypass, and tests never `put_env` `:stripe_api_url`, `:stripe_secret_key` or `:stripe_req_options`. Workshop tests pick one of three seams: `Dhc.StripeHTTPStub` for a test that stubs a few Stripe routes; `DhcWeb.WorkshopStripeClient` (a whole-Stripe `Req.Test` plug, `Req.Test.stub(Dhc.Stripe, DhcWeb.WorkshopStripeClient)`) for workshop controller contract tests that should run the live adapter; and `Dhc.Workshops.StripeStub` (the `:workshop_stripe_adapter`, app-env driven) for `PaymentCommands` workflow tests whose Stripe call runs outside the test's `$callers` tree (unboxed concurrency tasks) or must be paused. The one exception: real-Stripe `:integration` suites `put_env` a real `:stripe_secret_key` and reset `:stripe_req_options` to `[]` in setup (and restore both on exit); no other test changes Stripe config. Stubs reach Tasks/inline jobs via `$callers`; other processes need `Req.Test.allow/3`. Shared subscription-payment decoding lives in `Dhc.Stripe.SubscriptionPayment` and the one retry rule in `Dhc.Stripe.Failure.retryable?/1`; see "Stubbing Stripe" in `docs/agents/notes.md`.
- Keep generated Stripe modules under `lib/dhc/stripe/generated/` excluded from Credo instead of refactoring generated source
- Use the already included and available `:req` (`Req`) library for HTTP requests, **avoid** `:httpoison`, `:tesla`, and `:httpc`. Req is included by default and is the preferred HTTP client for Phoenix apps
- **Documented exception (ADR 0021)**: transactional email goes through Swoosh, whose api client is `config :swoosh, api_client: Dhc.Email.ApiClient` wrapping `Swoosh.ApiClient.Finch` over a named `{Finch, name: Swoosh.Finch}` child in `Dhc.Application`. Finch is already a production dependency, so Hackney stays out of prod. Application code outside `Dhc.Email.*` still uses Req everywhere else.
- Hackney is test-only because Testcontainers requires its 1.x Unix-socket transport. Keep it out of production and do not force Hackney 4 until Testcontainers supports Docker Unix sockets with it; the matching Hackney advisory exceptions in `mix.exs` apply only to that test dependency.
- Nostrum's REST client pulls Gun and Cowlib into production (Gun is floored at 2.7 in `mix.exs`, which resolves Cowlib 2.21 — fixed for CVE-2026-43971 and CVE-2026-43969). Limit Cowlib advisory exceptions to explicitly reviewed CVE IDs and document the relevant exposure or mitigation in `mix.exs`; keep ignoring CVE-2026-43966 only until a fixed Cowlib release ships, and keep the Hackney 4-only CVE exceptions (CVE-2026-47069/47071/47075/47076) only while Testcontainers requires Hackney 1.x.

### Phoenix v1.8 guidelines

- **Always** begin your LiveView templates with `<Layouts.app flash={@flash} ...>` which wraps all inner content
- The `MyAppWeb.Layouts` module is aliased in the `my_app_web.ex` file, so you can use it without needing to alias it again
- Anytime you run into errors with no `current_scope` assign:
  - You failed to follow the Authenticated Routes guidelines, or you failed to pass `current_scope` to `<Layouts.app>`
  - **Always** fix the `current_scope` error by moving your routes to the proper `live_session` and ensure you pass `current_scope` as needed
- Phoenix v1.8 moved the `<.flash_group>` component to the `Layouts` module. You are **forbidden** from calling `<.flash_group>` outside of the `layouts.ex` module
- Out of the box, `core_components.ex` imports an `<.icon name="hero-x-mark" class="w-5 h-5"/>` component for hero icons. **Always** use the `<.icon>` component for icons, **never** use `Heroicons` modules or similar
- **Always** use the imported `<.input>` component for form inputs from `core_components.ex` when available. `<.input>` is imported and using it will save steps and prevent errors
- If you override the default input classes (`<.input class="myclass px-2 py-1 rounded-lg">)`) class with your own values, no default classes are inherited, so your
custom classes must fully style the input


<!-- usage-rules-start -->

<!-- phoenix:elixir-start -->
## Elixir guidelines

- Elixir lists **do not support index based access via the access syntax**

  **Never do this (invalid)**:

      i = 0
      mylist = ["blue", "green"]
      mylist[i]

  Instead, **always** use `Enum.at`, pattern matching, or `List` for index based list access, ie:

      i = 0
      mylist = ["blue", "green"]
      Enum.at(mylist, i)

- Elixir variables are immutable, but can be rebound, so for block expressions like `if`, `case`, `cond`, etc
  you *must* bind the result of the expression to a variable if you want to use it and you CANNOT rebind the result inside the expression, ie:

      # INVALID: we are rebinding inside the `if` and the result never gets assigned
      if connected?(socket) do
        socket = assign(socket, :val, val)
      end

      # VALID: we rebind the result of the `if` to a new variable
      socket =
        if connected?(socket) do
          assign(socket, :val, val)
        end

- **Never** nest multiple modules in the same file as it can cause cyclic dependencies and compilation errors
- **Never** use map access syntax (`changeset[:field]`) on structs as they do not implement the Access behaviour by default. For regular structs, you **must** access the fields directly, such as `my_struct.field` or use higher level APIs that are available on the struct if they exist, `Ecto.Changeset.get_field/2` for changesets
- Elixir's standard library has everything necessary for date and time manipulation. Familiarize yourself with the common `Time`, `Date`, `DateTime`, and `Calendar` interfaces by accessing their documentation as necessary. The one sanctioned date/time dependency is `tz`, the IANA database behind `Dhc.ClubCalendar`'s Europe/Dublin conversions. **Never** install additional dependencies unless asked or for date/time parsing (which you can use the `date_time_parser` package)
- Don't use `String.to_atom/1` on user input (memory leak risk)
- Predicate function names should not start with `is_` and should end in a question mark. Names like `is_thing` should be reserved for guards
- Elixir's builtin OTP primitives like `DynamicSupervisor` and `Registry`, require names in the child spec, such as `{DynamicSupervisor, name: MyApp.MyDynamicSup}`, then you can use `DynamicSupervisor.start_child(MyApp.MyDynamicSup, child_spec)`
- Use `Task.async_stream(collection, callback, options)` for concurrent enumeration with back-pressure. The majority of times you will want to pass `timeout: :infinity` as option

## Mix guidelines

- Read the docs and options before using tasks (by using `mix help task_name`)
- To debug test failures, run tests in a specific file with `mix test test/my_test.exs` or run all previously failed tests with `mix test --failed`
- `mix deps.clean --all` is **almost never needed**. **Avoid** using it unless you have good reason

## Test guidelines

- **Always use `start_supervised!/1`** to start processes in tests as it guarantees cleanup between tests
- **Avoid** `Process.sleep/1` and `Process.alive?/1` in tests
  - Instead of sleeping to wait for a process to finish, **always** use `Process.monitor/1` and assert on the DOWN message:

      ref = Process.monitor(pid)
      assert_receive {:DOWN, ^ref, :process, ^pid, :normal}

   - Instead of sleeping to synchronize before the next call, **always** use `_ = :sys.get_state/1` to ensure the process has handled prior messages
<!-- phoenix:elixir-end -->

<!-- phoenix:phoenix-start -->
## Phoenix guidelines

- Remember Phoenix router `scope` blocks include an optional alias which is prefixed for all routes within the scope. **Always** be mindful of this when creating routes within a scope to avoid duplicate module prefixes.

- You **never** need to create your own `alias` for route definitions! The `scope` provides the alias, ie:

      scope "/admin", AppWeb.Admin do
        pipe_through :browser

        live "/users", UserLive, :index
      end

  the UserLive route would point to the `AppWeb.Admin.UserLive` module

- `Phoenix.View` no longer is needed or included with Phoenix, don't use it
<!-- phoenix:phoenix-end -->

<!-- phoenix:ecto-start -->
## Ecto Guidelines

- **Always** preload Ecto associations in queries when they'll be accessed in templates, ie a message that needs to reference the `message.user.email`
- Remember `import Ecto.Query` and other supporting modules when you write `seeds.exs`
- `Ecto.Schema` fields always use the `:string` type, even for `:text`, columns, ie: `field :name, :string`
- `Ecto.Changeset.validate_number/2` **DOES NOT SUPPORT the `:allow_nil` option**. By default, Ecto validations only run if a change for the given field exists and the change value is not nil, so such as option is never needed
- You **must** use `Ecto.Changeset.get_field(changeset, :field)` to access changeset fields
- Fields which are set programmatically, such as `user_id`, must not be listed in `cast` calls or similar for security purposes. Instead they must be explicitly set when creating the struct
- **Always** invoke `mix ecto.gen.migration migration_name_using_underscores` when generating migration files, so the correct timestamp and conventions are applied
<!-- phoenix:ecto-end -->

<!-- usage-rules-end -->

Read file docs/agents/commands.md, lines 1-150
1: # Commands
2: 
3: All tasks are defined in `.mise.toml`. Run `mise tasks` to list them all.
4: 
5: ## Setup
6: 
7: ```bash
8: # First time: install all pinned tools (Node, Erlang, Elixir, pnpm)
9: mise install
10: 
11: # Activate mise in your shell (one-time, add to your shell rc)
12: eval "$(mise activate bash)"    # bash
13: eval "$(mise activate zsh)"     # zsh
14: mise activate fish | source     # fish
15: ```
16: 
17: After activation, `node`, `elixir`, `mix`, `pnpm` etc. resolve to the versions pinned in `.mise.toml` on every `cd`.
18: 
19: ## SvelteKit (`apps/web`)
20: 
21: ```bash
22: # Dev (start in order)
23: docker compose up -d db mailpit   # 1. Start PostgreSQL + Mailpit (dev email catcher)
24: mise run phx-server               # 2. Phoenix API and Oban workers
25: mise run dev                      # 3. SvelteKit dev from apps/web

mix test

Alias for

    ["test --no-start"]

Location: mix.exs

There is also a task named "test". The documentation is shown next.


                                    mix test

Runs the tests for a project.

This task starts the current application, loads up `test/test_helper.exs` and
then, requires all files matching the `test/**/*_test.exs` pattern in parallel.

A list of files and/or directories can be given after the task name in order to
select the files to run:

    $ mix test test/some/particular/file_test.exs
    $ mix test test/some/particular/dir

Tests in umbrella projects can be run from the root by specifying the full
suite path, including `apps/my_app/test`, in which case recursive tests for
other child apps will be skipped completely:

    # To run all tests for my_app from the umbrella root
    $ mix test apps/my_app/test
    
    # To run a given test file on my_app from the umbrella root
    $ mix test apps/my_app/test/some/particular/file_test.exs

## Understanding test results

When you run your test suite, it prints results as they run with a summary at
the end, as seen below:

    $ mix test
    Running ExUnit with seed: 646219, max_cases: 16
    ...
    
      1) test greets the world (FooTest)
         test/foo_test.exs:5
         Assertion with == failed
         code:  assert Foo.hello() == :world!
         left:  :world
         right: :world!
         stacktrace:
           test/foo_test.exs:6: (test)
    
    ........
    
    Finished in 0.05 seconds (0.00s async, 0.05s sync)
    1 doctest, 11 tests, 1 failure

For each test, the test suite will print a dot. Failed tests are printed
immediately in the format described in the next section.

After all tests run, we print the suite summary. The first line contains the
total time spent on the suite, followed by how much time was spent on async
tests (defined with `use ExUnit.Case, async: true`) vs sync ones:

    Finished in 0.05 seconds (0.00s async, 0.05s sync)

Developers want to minimize the time spent on sync tests whenever possible, as
sync tests run serially and async tests run concurrently.

Finally, how many tests we have run, how many of them failed, how many were
invalid, and so on.

### Understanding test failures

First, it contains the failure counter, followed by the test name and the
module the test was defined:

    1) test greets the world (FooTest)

The next line contains the exact location of the test in the `FILE:LINE`
format:

    test/foo_test.exs:5

If you want to re-run only this test, all you need to do is to copy the line
above and paste it in front of `mix test`:

    $ mix test test/foo_test.exs:5

Then we show the error message, code snippet, and general information about the
failed test:

    Assertion with == failed
    code:  assert Foo.hello() == :world!
    left:  :world
    right: :world!

If your terminal supports coloring (see the  "Coloring" section below), a diff
is typically shown between `left` and `right` sides. Finally, we print the
stacktrace of the failure:

    stacktrace:
      test/foo_test.exs:6: (test)

## Command line options

  * `--all-warnings` (`--no-all-warnings`) - prints all warnings, including
    previous compilations (default is true except on errors)
  * `-b`, `--breakpoints` *(since v1.17.0)* - sets a breakpoint at the
    beginning of every test. The debugger goes line-by-line and can access all
    variables and imports (but not local functions). You can press `n` for the
    next line and `c` for the next test. This automatically sets `--trace`
  * `--color` - enables color in ExUnit formatting results
  * `--cover` - runs coverage tool. See "Coverage" section below
  * `--dry-run` *(since v1.19.0)* - prints which tests would be run based
    on current options, but does not actually run any tests. This combines with
    all other options like `--stale`, `--only`, `--exclude`, and so on.
  * `--exclude` - excludes tests that match the filter. This option may be
    given several times to apply different filters, such as `--exclude ci
    --exclude slow`. A value can also be provided for the filter such as
    `--exclude async:true` to only run the sync tests.
  * `--exit-status` - use an alternate exit status to use when the test
    suite fails (default is 2).
  * `--export-coverage` - the name of the file to export coverage results
    to. Only has an effect when used with `--cover`
  * `--failed` - runs only tests that failed the last time they ran
  * `--force` - forces compilation regardless of modification times
  * `--formatter` - sets the formatter module that will print the results.
    Defaults to ExUnit's built-in CLI formatter
  * `--include` - includes tests that match the filter. This option may be
    given several times to apply different filters, such as `--include ci
    --include slow`
  * `--listen-on-stdin` - runs tests, and then listens on stdin. It will
    re-run tests once a newline is received. See the "File system watchers"
    section below
  * `--max-cases` - sets the maximum number of tests running
    asynchronously. Only tests from different modules run in parallel. Defaults
    to twice the number of cores
  * `--max-failures` - the suite stops evaluating tests when this number of
    test failures is reached. It runs all tests if omitted
  * `--max-requires` - sets the maximum number of test files to compile in
    parallel. Setting this to `1` will compile test files sequentially.
  * `-n`, `--name-pattern` *(since v1.19.0)* - only run tests with names
    that match the given regular expression
  * `--no-archives-check` - does not check archives
  * `--no-color` - disables color in the output
  * `--no-compile` - does not compile, even if files require compilation
  * `--no-deps-check` - does not check dependencies
  * `--no-elixir-version-check` - does not check the Elixir version from
    `mix.exs`
  * `--no-start` - does not start applications after compilation
  * `--only` - runs only tests that match the filter. Such as `--only ci`.
    A value can also be provided for the filter such as `--only async:true` to
    only run the async tests.
  * `--partitions` - sets the amount of partitions to split tests in. It
    must be a number greater than zero. If set to one, it acts a no-op. If more
    than one, then you must also set the `MIX_TEST_PARTITION` environment
    variable with the partition to use in the current test run. See the
    "Operating system process partitioning" section for more information
  * `--preload-modules` - preloads all modules defined in applications
  * `--profile-require time` - profiles the time spent to require test
    files. Used only for debugging. The test suite does not run
  * `--raise` - immediately raises if the test suite fails, instead of
    continuing the execution of other Mix tasks
  * `--repeat-until-failure` *(since v1.17.0)* - sets the number of
    repetitions for running the suite until it fails. This is useful for
    debugging flaky tests within the same instance of the Erlang VM. For
    example, `--repeat-until-failure 10000` repeats the test suite up to 10 000
    times until the first failure. This can be combined with `--max-failures 1`
    to immediately stop if one test fails. However, if there is any leftover
    global state after running the tests, re-running the suite may trigger
    unrelated failures.
  * `--seed` - seeds the random number generator used to randomize the
    order of tests; `--seed 0` disables randomization so the tests in a single
    file will always be ran in the same order they were defined in
  * `--slowest` - prints timing information for the N slowest tests.
    Includes time spent in `ExUnit.Callbacks.setup/1`. Automatically sets
    `--trace` and `--preload-modules`
  * `--slowest-modules` *(since v1.17.0)* - prints timing information for
    the N slowest modules. Includes time spent in `ExUnit.Callbacks.setup/1`.
    Automatically sets `--trace` and `--preload-modules`
  * `--stale` - runs only tests which reference modules that changed since
    the last time tests were ran with `--stale`. You can read more about this
    option in the "The --stale option" section below
  * `--timeout` - sets the timeout for the tests
  * `--trace` - runs tests with detailed reporting. Automatically sets
    `--max-cases` to `1`. Note that in trace mode test timeouts will be ignored
    as timeout is set to `:infinity`
  * `--warnings-as-errors` *(since v1.12.0)* - treats compilation warnings
    (from loading the test suite) as errors and returns an exit status of 1 if
    the test suite would otherwise pass. If the test suite fails and also
    include warnings as errors, the exit status returned will be the value of
    the `--exit-status` option, which defaults to `2`, plus one. Therefore in
    the default case, this will be exit status `3`.
    Note that failures reported by `--warnings-as-errors` cannot be retried
    with the `--failed` flag.

    This option only applies to test files. To treat warnings as errors during
    compilation and during tests, run:

        MIX_ENV=test mix do compile --warnings-as-errors + test --warnings-as-errors


## Configuration

These configurations can be set in the `def project` section of your `mix.exs`:

  * `:test_coverage` - a set of options to be passed down to the coverage
    mechanism. See the "Coverage" section for more information
  * `:test_elixirc_options` - the compiler options to used when
    loading/compiling test files. By default it disables the debug chunk, docs
    chunk, and module type inference
  * `:test_paths` - list of paths containing test files. Defaults to
    `["test"]` if the `test` directory exists, otherwise, it defaults to `[]`.
    It is expected that all test paths contain a `test_helper.exs` file
  * `:test_pattern` - a pattern to find potential test files. Defaults to
    `"*.{ex,exs}"`.
    Once files are found, they are filtered in two ways:

    * Files that match `:test_load_filters` are loaded
    * Files that match `:test_ignore_filters` are ignored
    * All other files emit a warning

    In Elixir versions earlier than 1.19.0, this option defaulted to
    `*_test.exs`.

  * `:test_load_filters` - a list of files, regular expressions or
    one-arity functions to restrict which files matched by the `:test_pattern`
    are loaded. Defaults to `[&String.ends_with?(&1, "_test.exs")]`. Paths are
    relative to the project root and separated by `/`, even on Windows.
  * `:test_ignore_filters` - a list of files, regular expressions or
    one-arity functions to ignore by the loader. Any file that is not loaded
    and not ignored will emit a warning.
    Mix ignores files ending in `_helper.exs` by default, as well as any file
    included in the project's `:elixirc_paths`.

    For example, to ignore all files in a `test/support/` folder:

        def project do
          [
            ...,
            test_ignore_filters: [&String.starts_with?(&1, "test/support/")]
          ]
        end

    You may choose to disable all warnings by ignoring all files with `[fn _ ->
    true end]`.

    Paths are relative to the project root and separated by `/`, even on
    Windows.


## Coloring

Coloring is enabled by default on most Unix terminals. They are also available
on Windows consoles from Windows 10, although it must be explicitly enabled for
the current user in the registry by running the following command:

    $ reg add HKCU\Console /v VirtualTerminalLevel /t REG_DWORD /d 1

After running the command above, you must restart your current console.

## Tags and filters

ExUnit provides tags and filtering functionality that allow developers to
select which tests to run. The most common functionality is to exclude some
particular tests from running by default in your test helper file:

    # Exclude all external tests from running
    ExUnit.configure(exclude: [external: true])

Then, whenever desired, those tests could be included in the run via the
`--include` option:

    $ mix test --include external:true

The example above will run all tests that have the external option set to
`true`. It is also possible to include all examples that have a given tag,
regardless of its value:

    $ mix test --include external

Note that all tests are included by default, so unless they are excluded first
(either in the test helper or via the `--exclude` option) the `--include`
option has no effect. The order in which filters are applied is also
consistent: first all exclusions are computed, then the inclusions.

For convenience, Mix also provides an `--only` option that excludes all tests
and includes only the given ones:

    $ mix test --only external

Which is similar to:

    $ mix test --include external --exclude test

However, when the `--only` option is used and no tests run, the test run fails.

In case a single file is being tested, it is possible to pass one or more
specific line numbers to run only those given tests:

    $ mix test test/some/particular/file_test.exs:12

Which is equivalent to:

    $ mix test --exclude test --include line:12 test/some/particular/file_test.exs

Or:

    $ mix test test/some/particular/file_test.exs:12:24

Which is equivalent to:

    $ mix test --exclude test --include line:12 --include line:24 test/some/particular/file_test.exs

If a given line starts a `describe` block, that line filter includes all tests
within the describe. Otherwise, it runs the closest test on or before the given
line number.

## Coverage

Elixir provides built-in line-based test coverage via the `--cover` flag. The
test coverages shows which lines of code and in which files were executed
during the test run.

### Limitations

Elixir uses Erlang's `:cover` (`:cover`) for its default test coverage. Erlang
coverage is done by tracking *executable lines of code*. See `mix
test.coverage` for details.

### Configuration

The `:test_coverage` configures the coverage tool and the default tool accepts
the following options:

  * `:tool` - a module specifying the coverage tool to use. Defaults to
    `Mix.Tasks.Test.Coverage`.
  * `:output` - the output directory for cover results. Defaults to
    `"cover"`.
  * `:summary` - at the end of each coverage run, a summary of each module
    is printed, with results in red or green depending on whether the
    percentage is below or above a given threshold. The task will exit with
    status of 1 if the total coverage is below the threshold. The `:summary`
    option allows you to customize the summary generation and defaults to
    `[threshold: 90]`, but it may be set to `false` to disable such reports.
  * `:export` - a filename to export results to instead of generating the
    coverage result on the fly. The `.coverdata` extension is automatically
    added to the given file. This option is automatically set via the
    `--export-coverage` option or when using process partitioning. See `mix
    test.coverage` to compile a report from multiple exports.
  * `:ignore_modules` - modules to ignore from generating reports and in
    summaries. It is a list of module names as atoms and regular expressions
    that are matched against the module names.
  * `:local_only` - by default coverage only tracks local calls, set this
    option to false if you plan to run coverage across nodes.

By default, a wrapper around OTP's `cover` is used as the coverage tool. You
can learn more about how it works in the docs for `mix test.coverage`. Your
tool of choice can be given as follows:

    def project() do
      [
        ...
        test_coverage: [tool: CoverModule]
        ...
      ]
    end

`CoverModule` can be any module that exports `start/2`, receiving the
compilation path and the `test_coverage` options as arguments. It must return
either `nil` or an anonymous function of zero arity that will run after the
test suite is done.

## Operating system process partitioning

While ExUnit supports the ability to run tests concurrently within the same
Elixir instance, it is not always possible to run all tests concurrently. For
example, some tests may rely on global resources.

For this reason, `mix test` supports partitioning the test files across
different Elixir instances. This is done by setting the `--partitions` option
to an integer, with the number of partitions, and setting the
`MIX_TEST_PARTITION` environment variable to control which test partition that
particular instance is running. This can also be useful if you want to
distribute testing across multiple machines.

For example, to split a test suite into 4 partitions and run them, you would
use the following commands:

    $ MIX_TEST_PARTITION=1 mix test --partitions 4
    $ MIX_TEST_PARTITION=2 mix test --partitions 4
    $ MIX_TEST_PARTITION=3 mix test --partitions 4
    $ MIX_TEST_PARTITION=4 mix test --partitions 4

The test files are sorted upfront in a round-robin fashion. Note the partition
itself is given as an environment variable so it can be accessed in config
files and test scripts. For example, it can be used to setup a different
database instance per partition in `config/test.exs`.

If partitioning is enabled and `--cover` is used, no cover reports are
generated, as they only contain a subset of the coverage data. Instead, the
coverage data is exported to files such as
`cover/MIX_TEST_PARTITION.coverdata`. Once you have the results of all
partitions inside `cover/`, you can run `mix test.coverage` to get the unified
report.

## The --stale option

The `--stale` command line option attempts to run only the test files which
reference modules that have changed since the last time you ran this task with
`--stale`.

The first time this task is run with `--stale`, all tests are run and a
manifest is generated. On subsequent runs, a test file is marked "stale" if any
modules it references (and any modules those modules reference, recursively)
were modified since the last run with `--stale`. A test file is also marked
"stale" if it has been changed since the last run with `--stale`.

The `--stale` option is extremely useful for software iteration, allowing you
to run only the relevant tests as you perform changes to the codebase.

## File-system watchers

You can integrate `mix test` with file system watchers through the command line
via the `--listen-on-stdin` option. For example, you can use fswatch
(https://github.com/emcrisostomo/fswatch) or similar to emit newlines whenever
there is a change, which will cause your test suite to re-run:

    $ fswatch lib test | mix test --listen-on-stdin

This can be combined with the `--stale` option to re-run only the test files
that have changed as well as the tests that have gone stale due to changes in
`lib`.

## Aborting the suite

It is possible to abort the test suite with `Ctrl+\ `, which sends a SIGQUIT
signal to the Erlang VM. ExUnit will intercept this signal to show all tests
that have been aborted and print the results collected so far.

This can be useful in case the suite gets stuck and you don't want to wait
until the timeout times passes (which defaults to 30 seconds).
